nameStory: The "winged" in winged euonymus comes from the distinctive corky ridges that run along the stems, looking like little wings sprouting from the branches. The "burning bush" nickname refers to its spectacular fall display when the leaves turn brilliant shades of red and orange, appearing to glow like flames in the landscape.
description: Winged euonymus is a deciduous shrub that typically grows 6-10 feet tall and wide, forming a dense, rounded shape. Originally from Asia, it's become a popular landscaping plant throughout New England thanks to its stunning fall colors and neat growth habit. The shrub has small, unremarkable greenish flowers in spring, but makes up for it with bright pink-orange fruits and that famous fiery autumn display that earned it the "burning bush" nickname.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive corky "wings" - thin, flat ridges that run along the green to brown stems. Run your finger along a branch and you'll feel these papery projections that give the plant its name.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small oval leaves, 1-3 inches long, arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. They feel smooth and have a slightly waxy texture with fine-toothed edges that you can feel by running your finger along the margin.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright pink to reddish capsules about the size of a small pea split open in fall to reveal orange seeds. The colorful fruits dangle from thin stalks and persist after leaves drop.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a dense, rounded shrub with many branching stems from the base. The overall shape is quite symmetrical and tidy, making it popular for formal landscaping.

idTips.label: Fall Color
idTips.description: Leaves turn an intense, almost glowing red to pink-red that's hard to miss. The color is so vibrant it seems to light up from within, especially on sunny days.

habitat: Primarily found in residential landscapes, parks, and commercial plantings throughout New England as an ornamental shrub. It tolerates a wide range of soil conditions and light levels, from full sun to partial shade. While planted as a landscape ornamental, it can occasionally escape cultivation and establish in forest edges and disturbed areas.

seasonality.spring: Small, inconspicuous greenish-yellow flowers appear in clusters along the branches in May. New leaves emerge bright green and the corky wing ridges on stems are easily visible.
seasonality.summer: The plant looks fairly ordinary with small green leaves and developing fruits. The corky wings on the stems remain the most distinctive identifying feature during this season.
seasonality.fall: This is showtime! Leaves transform into brilliant reds, oranges, and pinks while bright pink fruits split open to reveal orange seeds. The fall display typically lasts 2-3 weeks in October.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches clearly show the corky wing ridges, and colorful pink seed capsules often persist into winter. The dense branching pattern and persistent fruits make identification possible even without leaves.

funFact: Despite its beautiful appearance, winged euonymus is considered invasive in many areas because birds love those colorful fruits and spread the seeds far and wide - a single shrub can produce thousands of seeds that remain viable in the soil for years, waiting for the right conditions to sprout!
confusionNotes: The corky winged stems make this shrub nearly impossible to confuse with anything else in New England. However, the fall color might remind you of sugar maple or other red-leafed trees, but the shrub size and those distinctive winged branches will set it apart immediately.
contextualKnowledge: Many gardeners don't realize that their beautiful "burning bush" is actually considered an invasive species in several New England states. While still sold in nurseries, some states restrict its sale, and conservation groups recommend native alternatives like elderberry or viburnum species for similar landscape effects.
compareHints: Among its Euonymus relatives in New England, winged euonymus is the only one with prominent corky wings on the stems. Fortune's spindle is a creeping evergreen groundcover, while European spindle is much less common and lacks the distinctive winged branches. The corky wing feature makes winged euonymus instantly recognizable among all the spindle species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike winged euonymus (burning bush) which is deciduous with prominent corky wing-like ridges on stems, Fortune's spindle stays evergreen and has smooth, round stems.
Unlike its notorious relative winged euonymus (burning bush), European spindle lacks the prominent corky 'wings' on its stems and has much less intense fall leaf color.
American wahoo differs from its cousin winged euonymus (burning bush) by lacking the distinctive corky wings on its stems and being much less common.
Among New England's euonymus species, Hamilton's spindle stands out for its four-lobed pink fruits and dangling orange seeds on threads.

Large-leaved spindle stands out from its New England relatives primarily by leaf size – its leaves are significantly larger than the small leaves of winged euonymus or the narrow leaves of other spindle species.
Unlike its deciduous relatives like winged euonymus (burning bush) or wahoo, Japanese spindle keeps its leaves year-round.
